messages.subject: Re: userGWAS: warning "some estimated ov variances are negative", NA Qsnp
messages.subject_clean: userGWAS: warning "some estimated ov variances are negative", NA Qsnp
messages.body_plain:
Hi Thanh Le,

Thanks for raising this! The new way of calculating factor-specific Qsnp uses as part of its calculation the difference (misfit) between the model implied SNP-trait covariances for the traits that load on that factor and the observed SNP-trait covariances. For a higher-order factor, those SNP-trait covariances are not observed for the lower-order factor used to define it, so the code is not currently written to be able to calculate Qsnp for higher-order factors. This is something that I've now documented on the wiki for this argument as below:
"Note that this will not produce Q_SNP statistics for higher-order factors (i.e., latent factors defined by lower-order latent factors). For higher-order factors the Q_SNP statistic can be calculated by using the model chi-square difference test across the model where the SNP predicts the higher-order factor compared to a model where the SNP predicts the indicators of the higher-order factor."

As noted there, you can still calculate Q_SNP for your F2 factor, but this will require running a second model where the SNP predicts the indicators of F2.

Best,
 Andrew

messages.subject: Re: Runtime for multivariate GWAS with large number of traits and SNPs
messages.subject_clean: Runtime for multivariate GWAS with large number of traits and SNPs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Pashupati,

There are two main things you can to do when you have that many SNPs:
1. The estimated model for each SNP is independent of all other SNPs, so you can split the runs up as much as is possible (e.g., by submitting different batches of SNPs to different jobs on a computing cluster).

2. If you can, run in parallel using multiple cores (ideally within separate jobs).

Best,
  Andrew

messages.body_plain:
Hi Maryam,

The traits listed in the LDSC step should be the munged files (with the .sumstats.gz file ending). It looks like you are providing the original GWAS files, which is throwing the error. If you are unable to find the files being created by the prior munge step I would suggest being sure to set your working directory prior to running that piece of code.

Best,
  Andrew

messages.subject_clean: userGWAS Error in eigen(V_full) : infinite or missing values in 'x'
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am trying to run a multivariate GWAS with 5 traits. The munge, LDSC, and sumstats preparation steps all completed without issue, but I am running into the following error:

Error in eigen(V_full) : infinite or missing values in 'x'
Calls: userGWAS -> .userGWAS_main -> eigen
Execution halted

I am running this GWAS stratified by chromosome, and I'm testing with chromosome 22.
The first time I saw this error, the function completes >3000 models before failing. Based on some other threads, I tried removing SNPs from the sumstats output that may have had problematic standard errors (0s). After doing this, the function ran over 90,000 models before failing again.

I am not sure how to continue troubleshooting what may be happening, or where the issues are coming from. Any help or ideas would be appreciated.

John

Regarding these issues, there are a few questions I had about methods and performance, and I thought I would include more information about my task.

I have 5 traits, the SNP numbers range from about 10 million to 13.8 million across these traits. I've run munge, ldsc, and sumstats preparation with these traits together with no issues. As far as I can tell, the output from LDSC looks fine.

I've tried running a userGWAS with both a single factor and 2-factor model on a Linux HPC cluster. Initially, the single factor timed out after 72 hours with 24 cores. To try and improve runtime performance I tried running separate jobs for each chromosome, where I use the full-genome LDSC results and subset my full-genome sumstats object for the current chromosome as follows:

sumstats_chr <- sumstats[ sumstats $CHR == chr, ]
# Run userGWAS on the chromosome-specific data
gwas_output <- userGWAS(
    covstruc = LDSCoutput,     # LDSC data loaded here
    estimation = "DWLS",
    SNPs =  sumstats_chr ,
    model = model_snp,
    parallel = FALSE
)

This method lead to my above errors with infinite or missing values in V_full.

My most recent effort was returning to the full-genome analysis and implementing the Linux performance fix that is noted in the documentation:

export OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 NUMEXPR_NUM_THREADS=1 VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS=1
~/anaconda3/envs/r-env/bin/R --no-echo --no-restore --file=gwas_template_full.R

These have been running overnight - I'm curious what the expected runtime would be for my 5 traits with ~10 million SNPs and 22 cores?

Best,
John

messages.subject: calculate effective sample size per SNP
messages.subject_clean: calculate effective sample size per SNP
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,
I used the formula provided in the GSEM wiki  (https://github.com/GenomicSEM/GenomicSEM/wiki/2.1-Calculating-Sum-of-Effective-Sample-Size-and-Preparing-GWAS-Summary-Statistics )to calculate the effective sample size per SNP for a few binary traits. Note that I have imbalances in case/control proportions per trait and non-independence among participants.

 In particular, I used this line of code as the template:  <ANX$Neff<-4/((2*ANX$MAF*(1-ANX$MAF))*ANX$StdErr^2)>,  and did not do the capping as i have already filtered markers based on quality and MAF, but the results were quite off (i.e., the resulted N effect is ~100 times larger than the total number of participants).

if I add the capping indicated in the GSEM, the yielded effective sample size per snp is too small for reliable sub-sequential analysis. I wonder if there are some other ways to calculate effective sample size per SNP so that I can cross check my results.
Thank you very much!
Lydia
